blocks.text: time and effort is focused around learning enough to reach the point where we can go out and get a job.
However, that’s not the end. The next 40 years is where the real challenge lies, and it’s not that easy.
The reason why is that jobs don’t usually line up with our passions, and there are so many different things out there to do.
How do we pick a profession that’s meaningful, that pays enough, and that lets us get home before 9 at night?
To do that, we need to find something to spend our lives on.
We need a calling that we can be excited about.
What’s a calling? A calling is a profession that’s so ingrained with your passions, your values, your sense of purpose, that the distinction between your job and your life is blurry.
In essence, your calling is what you want to do with your life.
Why does everyone have a calling?
Most people don’t realize this, but everyone has their own calling in life, waiting for them to do something with it.
A calling could be something as simple as wanting to be a doctor, but it could also be something as strange as solving the problem of gravity.
Some people find their calling early on in life and they pursue it happily every day.
Some people find their calling, but they don’t take action, and they don’t know why they are so drawn to that one thing.
Some people search their whole lives and never find it.
In the end, we all have it in us to do something with our lives, to make an impact on someone else’s life.
Sometimes it’s huge, and sometimes it’s small.

It is normal to want to defend yourself, your beliefs or to get defensive when being wrong is the conclusion.

I especially don’t like it when I think I am right, but later am proven to be wrong.
We all have these stubborn tendencies, which is why it is important to practice being wrong when you know you are wrong.

blocks.text: a blog, I had a choice: either I was going to follow the model of a lot of other scholars by posting mostly about my area of scholarly expertise, or I was going to have a general interest blog.
I chose the latter because, like many people, I am a generalist at heart.

What the hell, I thought. If a few people are interested in my blog posts on, say, 19th-century US History and Pragmatist Philosophy, they can read them, but I don’t want to restrict the subject matter of my writing to topics that I do scholarly research on.
But this being a blog and not a scholarly article, you’re probably wondering why you should read this post.
What’s the big deal about the fact that pragmatism (a movement in 19th-century US philosophy) took the subject of truth and replaced it with a different one: knowing?

I’ll try to explain this in two ways: (1) by making explicit my general interest in understanding what counts as knowledge or truth in general, and (2) by linking pragmatism’s change of subjects to a concern about “the achievements of human powers and practices,” which I assume are things that we generally want to get right.
The fact is that we do want to get things right.
That’s what’s called being honest and truthful, or even just getting things “straight” as in “getting a straight A,” or even “saying something straight” without beating around the bush.
And we usually define being truthful or honest as telling the truth, not telling lies.
What counts as a lie? A lie is something that’s untrue, so we can think of it in that sense as the opposite of the truth.
But if the subject of truth has been changed, by changing it to “knowing” or “knowledge” how can we identify what’s a lie?

blocks.text: learned from others while developing my own style.
So many wonderful writers out there can teach us how to love our own words.
I hope you’ll be inspired to write.
END NOTE Some of the best writing I’ve ever read has been short.
The power within a well-written paragraph is strong.
The more that you study the masters of short stories and essays, the more you understand the idea of the power within a short piece of writing.
I think there are many misconceptions surrounding what the short story, short essay, or memoir actually is.
I think, for the most part, that short story or short essay writers can agree upon what the differences are and what it takes for a short piece to be effective.
A poem can certainly take on a story-like form, but the main difference is that poems are more focused on image and rhythm.
Poems have the power to take you right to a place, a time, a memory, a moment, with the fewest words possible.
An essay can, of course, also be a story, but the main difference is that, in a piece of short writing, the writer has a clear purpose.
The essay, short story, and memoir, though similar, have slightly differing purposes and structures.
The memoir is a piece of writing that, more than anything, needs a purpose.
You are telling your life story; in many ways, you are reliving a period of your life and sharing those experiences with others.
Memoirs often take the reader through the course of an entire lifetime.
Some memoirs focus on certain points in the life of the writer.
Memoirs have the power to connect readers to the experiences of the writer.
When you create a memoir, you are also creating a bond with the people who read your words.

Finally, in what must have been some divine intervention, I finished writing the manuscript just two weeks before the conference.
It was a thrill, but when I uploaded it to the conference website, I realized I had two additional hurdles in front of me.
First, I had to pay for the evaluation.
It was costly, especially since I was unemployed at the time.
Second, the evaluation had to be finished before the conference.
If it wasn’t, no agents would be able to review it.
That’s the point of the evaluation, after all: to provide a rough draft, with potential areas for improvement, before you pitch your work to publishers.
I paid my money and waited. Fortunately, the evaluation was ready just in time.
After the conference, I uploaded the manuscript to the website and waited again, this time for the opportunity to submit to agents.
This was another costly endeavor, and I had to wait for a while to be able to afford it.
When the opportunity finally came, I submitted the manuscript and waited for a response.
Two weeks later, I received my first acceptance.
I was ecstatic, but it was just the beginning.
I had to go through a series of revisions and interviews with the agent to finalize the deal.
In the end, it took over a year to find a publisher, but I had accomplished my goal: a full manuscript in two months, followed by publication less than two years later.

blocks.text: , so I want to share them with you.
This is my personal interpretation, so it may differ from yours.
For that matter, some people believe that Buddha, dharma and sangha are not something we can recite, but they’re just actions we take.
But I think words matter, so I want to give you a brief summary of what the three refuges mean to me, and why I’ve added the fourth.
The Buddha When I say “Buddha,” the word means “awakened one.” It’s not a person.

It’s a title. The word “Buddha” in Sanskrit means “one who is awake.” A buddha is someone who’s no longer asleep to their own suffering and the suffering of others, and no longer deluded by their thoughts and feelings.
Many teachers are buddhas because they’re awake to their own suffering and the suffering of others.
They don’t think they’re enlightened; that’s another word entirely.
But they have more compassion and love for humanity because they’ve awakened.
They’re less attached to a small, egocentric world.
They think bigger, and it’s that compassion and love that inspires many of us to learn about the Dharma and join a sangha.
For me, my guru, Jack Kornfield, is a Buddha.
He’s awakened to suffering, but he’s not deluded about it.
He hasn’t let his thoughts and feelings blind him.
He has great love and compassion and is more interested in helping others than in gaining more followers.
Jack inspires me to go deeper, to wake up more to suffering, and to take better care of myself so I can help others.
